This is a sheep in the wild.

Domesticated sheep (most breeds, anyway) have been bred to shed as little wool as possible so that it can be sheered off of the sheep when convenient. Wild sheep (and some domesticated breeds) shed their wool every year. Around the time of domestication and persisting into various periods in various regions, sheep were allowed to naturally shed their wool and it was then collected for use (felting or spinning if the fibers weren't too matted) from the environment when it stuck to trees, etc. until people began to realize it was much simpler to get a lot of usable wool if you catch the sheep and cut all of the wool off of them at once. This led to selecting breeding stock that retained their wool for increasing lengths of time. Many modern breeds rarely shed their wool and what wool breaks off is typically so tightly bound within the other fibers as to remain trapped. This is a terrible feature to have if no one bothers to sheer, though.
